newsitem.title: USA: Jewish group defers decision on Swiss bank boycott.
newsitem.headline: Jewish group defers decision on Swiss bank boycott.

text.p: A Jewish group on Friday delayed deciding whether to urge a boycott of Swiss banks over their treatment of Holocaust victims as a Swiss diplomat said he had persuaded U.S. officials not to support such a move.

Swiss diplomat Thomas Borer, who heads a government task force examining whether Swiss banks still hold millions of dollars in unclaimed accounts from Holocaust victims, told reporters he thought he had persuaded congressional leaders this week that Switzerland sincerely sought the truth.

"We take this issue seriously. I convinced (the leaders) that we are doing the right thing and the question of a boycott should be off the table. They should give us time and if we don't do something, they would be justified," he said.

Borer made his comments after a cordial one-hour meeting with Switzerland's chief congressional critic, New York Republican Senator Alfonse D'Amato, head of the Senate Banking Committee. The two pledged to cooperate with each other.

Meanwhile, the World Jewish Congress, which has been spearheading a battle with Swiss banks over the disposition of Holocaust accounts, said it had decided to delay until late January a decision on whether to call for an international boycott of Swiss banks.
The WJC has been considering boycott calls from members who are dissatisfed with the Swiss banks' efforts to comb their files and find dormant accounts and Nazi loot.

Kalman Sultanik, a WJC vice president, said the group was delaying a decision because Borer had pledged in congressional testimony on Thursday to turn over a list of people whose dormant deposits in Swiss banks had been given to Poland.

Poland received almost 500,000 Swiss francs from the Swiss in the 1970s under a 1949 treaty in which Switzerland agreed to give Poland the dormant accounts in Swiss banks of Polish citizens. The Poles are believed to have used a small part of the money to pay Swiss citizens' property claims.

Most of the Polish accounts are thought to have belonged to Polish Jews but the Swiss have never revealed the names of the holders, arguing that it would have been dangerous to do so during the Cold War, although Poland was legally obligated to return the funds either to the owners or their survivors.

The Swiss national bank was reported on Friday to have admitted that it profited in dealings in looted Nazi gold during the Second World War but said none of it had come from concentration camp victims.
